tldr: ScienceAgentBench is a benchmark of 102 code generation tasks extracted from 44 peer-reviewed publications across four disciplines, used to rigorously evaluate LLM-based agents for data-driven scientific discovery; results show current agents can only solve ~32-42% of tasks even with multiple attempts.
contributions: ScienceAgentBench: a benchmark of 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed publications in Bioinformatics, Computational Chemistry, Geographical Information Science, and Psychology & Cognitive Neuroscience
Multi-metric evaluation framework including Valid Execution Rate, Success Rate, CodeBERTScore, API Cost, GPT-4o figure evaluation, and rubric-based grading
Two strategies to mitigate data contamination and agent shortcut concerns (removing test data points and replacing test labels with dummy values)
Comprehensive evaluation of five LLMs across three agent frameworks (direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct, self-debug)
methods: Tasks were annotated from peer-reviewed publications by nine graduate students following five steps: identifying self-contained code examples, collecting/preprocessing datasets, annotating reference programs, implementing success criteria, and writing instructions. Nine subject matter experts validated each task through a questionnaire covering realism, accuracy, supplementary knowledge, and rubric refinement. Two additional contamination mitigation strategies were applied: randomly removing five test data points and replacing test labels with dummy values for model development tasks. Five LLMs (Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B/405B, Mistral-Large-2-123B, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) were evaluated with direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct, and self-debug frameworks, each given three attempts per task.
results: The best-performing agent solved 32.4% of tasks independently and 34.3% with expert-provided knowledge (across three attempts per task). Claude-3.5-Sonnet with self-debug solved 10.8% more tasks than with OpenHands CodeAct while costing 17 times less in API fees. OpenAI o1-preview achieved 42.2% performance with direct prompting and self-debug, but at over 10 times the cost of other LLMs. Even with expert-provided knowledge, agents fell short of utilizing it effectively.
limitations: Scale of 102 tasks is smaller than benchmarks with synthetic or easier tasks, though justified by annotation difficulty and evaluation cost
Rubric-based evaluation currently requires human evaluation and has not yet been automated (e.g., with an LLM-based judge)
Agents still cannot automate essential tasks in data-driven discovery, let alone end-to-end research pipelines
